import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Imaginary part of $\prod_{k=0}^n (1 + k \cdot i)$, $i = \sqrt{-1}$

*References:*
- [A105751](https://oeis.org/A105751)
-/

open Complex Filter Topology Nat

namespace OeisA105751

/--
The primary defining sequence `a`.
a n is the imaginary part of $\prod_{k=0}^n (1 + k \cdot i)$, where $i = \sqrt{-1}$.
-/
noncomputable def a (n : ℕ) : ℤ :=
  let productTerm (k : ℕ) : ℂ := 1 + (k : ℂ) * I
  Int.floor (((Finset.range (n + 1)).prod productTerm).im)

/-- Term theorems verifying the first few values of the sequence against the official OEIS b-file -/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_0 : a 0 = 0 := by
  delta a; norm_num [Finset.prod]

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_1 : a 1 = 1 := by
  delta a; norm_num [Finset.prod]

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_2 : a 2 = 3 := by
  delta a; norm_num [Finset.prod]

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_3 : a 3 = 0 := by
  delta a; norm_num [Finset.prod]

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_4 : a 4 = -40 := by
  delta a; norm_num [Finset.prod]

/--
Numerical calculation suggests that a similar division holds in this case.
Type 1: primes p that do not divide any element of the sequence {$a(n)$}.
In this case, unlike in A105750, the set of type 1 primes is empty;
that is, every prime p divides some term of this sequence.

Note: The triangular number n*(n+1)/2 divides $a(n)$ (see A164652).
In particular, if $p$ is an odd prime then $p$ divides $a(p)$. For $p=2$, $2$ divides $a(4)=-40$.
-/
@[category textbook, AMS 11]
theorem prime_divides_some_term (p : ℕ) (hp : p.Prime) :
    ∃ n : ℕ, (p : ℤ) ∣ a n := by
  sorry

/--
Moll's conjecture 5.5 extends to this sequence and takes the form:
(i) the $2$-adic valuation $\nu_2(a(n)) \sim n/4$ as n -> oo.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11,
  formal_proof using formal_conjectures at
    "https://github.com/KitaKen1/oeis-a105751-two-adic/blob/a9692d90078c4dff1478acaaa70be2fba06a3ef9/lean/OeisA105751TwoAdicFC.lean#L980-L985"]
theorem conjecture :
    Tendsto (fun n ↦ (4 : ℚ) * (padicValInt 2 (a n) : ℚ) / (n : ℚ)) atTop (nhds 1) := by
  sorry

/--
Moll's conjecture 5.5 extends to this sequence and takes the form:
(ii) for the other primes of type $2$, the p-adic valuation
$\nu_p(a(n)) \sim n/(p - 1)$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$.

(Type 2 primes consists of primes p == 1 (mod 4))
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem conjecture.variants.moll_p_mod_4_eq_1 {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) (h_mod : p % 4 = 1) :
    Tendsto (fun n ↦ ((p - 1 : ℚ) * (padicValInt p (a n) : ℚ)) / (n : ℚ)) atTop (nhds 1) := by
  sorry

end OeisA105751

findings.description: The parenthetical on line 89 says that type-2 primes consist of primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4), omitting the exceptional type-2 prime 2. The theorem's restriction is correct for part (ii), since 2 is treated by the preceding theorem; only the parenthetical is inaccurate.
findings.source_evidence: OEIS A105751, Peter Bala's comments of June 1, 2023, conjectures that the type-2 primes are the primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4) 'together with the prime p = 2'. Read in the official OEIS data mirror: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/oeis/oeisdata/main/seq/A105/A105751.seq.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the parenthetical with: 'The other type-2 primes are conjecturally the primes p ≡ 1 (mod 4); the exceptional prime 2 is treated above.'

reformulations.difference: Lean takes the integer floor of the imaginary part, whereas OEIS directly defines the sequence as that imaginary part.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every factor 1 + k*i is a Gaussian integer, so the product's imaginary part is an integer. Integer floor therefore changes nothing, including for negative terms. In scratch.lean I proved the Gaussian-integer identification and the explicit equivalence a n = z ↔ (z : ℝ) = Im(∏_{k=0}^n (1+k*i)).

reformulations.difference: Lean expresses ν₂(a(n)) ∼ n/4 as convergence of 4*ν₂(a(n))/n to 1 in ℚ, using a valuation that returns 0 at zero.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The usual topology on ℚ is induced by its embedding into ℝ, and 4*ν₂(a(n))/n equals ν₂(a(n))/(n/4). Since n/4 is eventually nonzero, convergence of this ratio to 1 is equivalent to the stated real asymptotic equivalence; this ↔ was proved in scratch.lean. Using the cited proof's exact-valuation lemmas, nonzero.lean also proves a n = 0 iff n = 0 or n = 3, without sorryAx. Thus the valuation's zero convention and division at n = 0 affect only finitely many indices.

reformulations.difference: Lean uses a rational normalized limit instead of the source's real asymptotic notation ν_p(a(n)) ∼ n/(p−1).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For each fixed prime p, p−1 is positive. The expression (p−1)*ν_p(a(n))/n equals ν_p(a(n))/(n/(p−1)), and rational convergence to 1 is equivalent to real convergence to 1. I proved the resulting ↔ in scratch.lean. The prime and congruence hypotheses are satisfiable (p=5), and the zero terms at indices 0 and 3 do not affect the limit.

review.notes: All nine declarations were checked. Apart from the minor parenthetical slip, the mathematical statements are faithful. The computable Gaussian-integer representation, proved equal to a, matches all 451 b-file entries. The five test theorems have only standard Lean axioms. prime_divides_some_term is indeed trivial with witness n=0, even without primality, but this matches OEIS's literal statement about divisibility of some term and is not a misformalization of an open claim. The cited 2-adic proof compiles against this checkout and its target depends only on propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, supporting the solved status. OEIS continues to state the other-prime asymptotic as a conjecture. OEIS's main HTML entry was blocked by a browser challenge, so its full entry was read through the official data mirror. Experiments are in /workspace/review/; the reviewed file remains identical to the specified commit.
